strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution by questioning whether successful downstream performance demonstrates generalization in weight generation. Its evaluations of image classifiers and neural fields are relevant to computer vision, and the proposed accuracy–novelty comparisons could improve evaluation practices.

The strongest memorization findings have complementary support from weight distances, functional comparisons, and additional examples selected across distance percentiles. For HyperDiffusion, 94.4% of generated checkpoints lie within L2 distance 10 of a training checkpoint, whereas all training pairs are separated by more than 50; reconstructed shapes also closely resemble training examples.

The simple baselines are informative and practically useful. Noise addition matches the reported performance–novelty trade-offs of several generators, while checkpoint averaging provides a competitive baseline for P-diff. The Hyper-Representations comparison appropriately accounts for its selection of high-performing checkpoints.

The investigation goes beyond nearest-neighbor illustrations: Table 1 examines training duration, capacity, and regularization, and Section 4.2 tests symmetry handling. The appendix supplies alternative behavioral measurements, additional visualizations, and method-specific evaluation details.
Overall, the supported diagnostic findings and inexpensive baselines favor acceptance. The contribution remains valuable despite reservations about interpreting all observed behavior as memorization.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is too uniform across methods. P-diff improves both accuracy and behavioral novelty over its training checkpoints and outperforms noise addition. Matching its performance with averaging establishes a strong baseline, but does not establish that its generation mechanism merely interpolates. Coordinate-wise marginal distributions and t-SNE plots do not demonstrate joint-space interpolation; independent Gaussian sampling is not generally a convex interpolation either.

P-diff's comparison with independently trained networks is not a matched test of generalization. Appendix A states that only the last two batch-normalization layers are generated, with the remaining network fixed. Much greater diversity among independently trained full networks is therefore expected. A reference distribution obtained by independently adapting the same parameter subset from the same backbone would better contextualize the observed novelty. The references also differ in mean accuracy: 75.4% versus 76.8%.

Some behavioral evidence supports narrower conclusions than the text suggests. In Table 2, G.pt's generated-to-training prediction overlap is 98.2%, compared with 97.9% between training neighbors—a small separation. For Hyper-Representations, comparisons primarily use autoencoder reconstructions rather than original training weights, so the evidence establishes proximity to decoded training representations more directly than reproduction of the original checkpoints. These distinctions matter when claiming nearly universal replication.

The baseline comparisons rely mainly on scatter plots of 100 samples per type, without uncertainty estimates or quantitative summaries of performance at matched novelty. This is sufficient to reveal large effects, but weaker support for claims of equivalence or 'no significant difference,' especially for HyperDiffusion. Nearest-test-shape Chamfer distance also does not fully characterize shape quality or distribution coverage.

The mitigation and cross-domain conclusions exceed the tested scope. Table 1 evaluates a limited set of settings using weight-space L2 rather than the behavioral novelty criterion central to Section 3. The Flowers comparison matches sample count but not architecture, distribution complexity, or optimization conditions. These experiments document failures under the tested configurations, rather than establishing that conventional mitigation cannot work or that weight generation is intrinsically less generalizable.

Reproducibility is only partial. Although Appendix A identifies checkpoints and source implementations, the manuscript does not fully specify several modifications, including noise injection details and exact architecture changes, or explain how exhaustive permutation matching is implemented. The abstract's project-page/code statement also has no visible link. These are correctable reporting weaknesses rather than reasons by themselves to reject.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution: downstream accuracy or reconstruction quality alone can conceal substantial copying in weight generators. This is relevant to image classification and neural-field generation, even without proposing a new model.

The strongest evidence is convincing. For HyperDiffusion, 94.4% of generated checkpoints are within L2 distance 10 of a training checkpoint, whereas all training pairs exceed 50. Closely matching reconstructed shapes corroborate this finding in function space rather than relying solely on parameter distance.

The noise and weight-averaging baselines are informative practical controls. Figures 6 and 8 show that inexpensive alternatives can achieve comparable accuracy–novelty trade-offs, questioning the added value of the evaluated generators.

The investigation includes four methods, architecture and regularization ablations, symmetry experiments, and supplementary examples selected by distance percentile. These provide substantially more support than isolated nearest-neighbor visualizations. Overall, the supported diagnostic contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about the broader interpretation.
weaknesses: The paper sometimes conflates replication, interpolation, and failure to generalize. This is most consequential for P-diff: generated models improve accuracy and differ behaviorally from training checkpoints. Matching averaging baselines establishes limited added value, but does not itself establish memorization. Marginal parameter histograms and t-SNE do not demonstrate that generated vectors are interpolations; independently sampling fitted Gaussian marginals is not necessarily interpolation either.

Some comparisons do not cleanly isolate memorization. Hyper-Representations is compared primarily against autoencoder reconstructions, whose accuracy is substantially degraded, so the results cannot distinguish copying original checkpoints from concentration induced by the decoder. Appendix A also reveals that P-diff generates only the last two batch-normalization layers; comparing its diversity with independently trained full networks introduces variation outside the generator's scope.

Behavioral evidence is uneven across methods. In Table 2, G.pt's generated-to-training prediction overlap is 98.2%, compared with 97.9% between training neighbors—a small difference without uncertainty estimates. Error-set IoU is useful but also reflects shared task difficulty. Thus, the strong HyperDiffusion result should not be interpreted as equally strong evidence of replication for every method.

The baseline comparisons mainly use scatterplots of 100 samples with selected noise amplitudes. They lack repeated-run uncertainty or quantitative comparisons at matched novelty. For shapes, nearest-test-shape Chamfer distance is also an imperfect quality measure: resembling a held-out shape does not fully establish plausibility or distributional coverage.

The mitigation conclusions exceed the tested settings. Table 1 explores a finite selection of configurations and uses parameter L2 rather than the behavioral novelty measures emphasized earlier. Likewise, the Flowers comparison changes architecture, representation, and data distribution along with modality, so it does not isolate why image and weight generators behave differently.

Reproducibility is helped by Appendix A and references to official implementations, but the submitted manuscript lacks the advertised project/code URL and sufficient details for some custom experiments, including Gaussian training-noise magnitude and the procedure for exhaustive permutation matching. These are correctable reporting limitations.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution: downstream accuracy or reconstruction quality alone can conceal replication of training checkpoints. This is relevant to evaluating weight generators for visual classifiers and neural fields, even without proposing a new generation method.

The strongest findings are supported by complementary evidence rather than selected examples alone. For HyperDiffusion, 94.4% of generated checkpoints lie within L2 distance 10 of a training checkpoint, while training pairs are separated by more than 50. Behavioral comparisons and examples across distance percentiles reinforce the weight-space results.

The simple baselines are informative and reasonably constructed. Noise addition tests whether generation improves the accuracy–novelty trade-off, while checkpoint averaging and Gaussian sampling offer practical alternatives for P-diff. Appendix C.2 appropriately matches Hyper-Representations’ selection of high-performing source checkpoints.

The study spans four substantially different methods and includes meaningful investigations of training duration, model capacity, regularization, and symmetry augmentation. These analyses make the paper more useful than a demonstration of isolated copying. Overall, the supported diagnostic contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about interpretation and scope.
weaknesses: The P-diff evidence establishes limited diversity and competitive simple baselines more convincingly than it establishes memorization or interpolation. Marginal parameter distributions and t-SNE proximity do not show that generated vectors are interpolations of training vectors; independent Gaussian sampling is not generally interpolation either. Figure 6 explicitly shows improved accuracy and behavioral novelty over training checkpoints. Calling this absence of meaningful generalization requires a more precise criterion.

The conclusions sometimes exceed the evaluated scope. Appendix A specifies one main setting per method: SVHN for Hyper-Representations, MNIST for G.pt, ShapeNet airplanes for HyperDiffusion, and only the last two batch-normalization layers of ResNet-18 for P-diff. The latter restriction is particularly important when interpreting comparisons with independently trained networks. These experiments support findings about the tested configurations, rather than weight generation generally.

Some measurements require more cautious interpretation. Hyper-Representations is compared primarily against autoencoder reconstructions, whose performance is substantially degraded; this demonstrates similarity to decoded training representations rather than direct replication of original checkpoints. For G.pt, Table 2 shows only a small prediction-overlap difference between generated-to-training and training-to-training comparisons, 98.2% versus 97.9%. Thus, the behavioral evidence is not equally strong across methods.

The mitigation conclusions are broader than the finite ablations establish. Table 1 tests a limited range and switches to L2 distance as the novelty proxy without behavioral validation of those variants. Reducing HyperDiffusion width increases distance from 7.03 to 22.47 while MMD changes from 0.036 to 0.039, illustrating a trade-off that deserves qualification. The results show that the tested adjustments do not close the observed gap, rather than that such strategies cannot mitigate memorization.

Uncertainty and reproducibility reporting are incomplete. The principal baseline comparisons use scatter plots of 100 samples without repeated-generator training results or uncertainty estimates for matched-novelty performance. The manuscript also leaves the claimed project/code URL blank and does not sufficiently specify the exhaustive permutation-matching procedure or all modified training settings. These limitations matter most for close baseline comparisons and reproducing the ablations, rather than the largest observed replication effects.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution by separating downstream performance from novelty in generated network weights. This is relevant to both image classification and neural-field generation, and the findings challenge evaluation practices without requiring a new state-of-the-art method.

The central evidence for near-copying is convincing, particularly for HyperDiffusion: 94.4% of generated checkpoints lie within L2 distance 10 of training weights, whereas training pairs are more than 50 apart. Weight comparisons, reconstructed shapes, percentile-based examples, and the data-copying tests in Appendix B provide complementary support.

The simple baselines are valuable. Noise addition exposes limited benefits from several generators, while weight averaging and fitted Gaussian sampling substantially reproduce p-diff's accuracy–novelty trade-off. The paper explicitly acknowledges that p-diff outperforms the noise baseline.

The investigation goes substantially beyond selected visual examples. Data scaling, random-weight experiments, architecture and regularization ablations, an ImageNet p-diff experiment, and alternative behavioral metrics strengthen the analysis. G.pt's improvement after scaling from 2.1M to 20.4M checkpoints provides a constructive counterpoint to the negative findings.

Overall, the supported empirical audit warrants weak acceptance. Its practical evaluation lessons remain valuable despite reservations about the interpretation of interpolation and the proposed explanations for memorization.
weaknesses: The claim that p-diff generates by interpolation 'not generalization' is stronger than the evidence establishes. Concentrated parameter marginals, t-SNE proximity, and comparable baseline performance do not demonstrate that generated vectors are interpolations of training checkpoints. Independent Gaussian sampling is also not generally a convex interpolation. These results establish a lack of demonstrated advantage over simple alternatives more clearly than they establish memorization or absence of generalization.

Behavioral evidence varies materially across methods. In Table 4, G.pt's generated-to-training prediction overlap is 98.2%, compared with 97.9% between training models, a small difference that does not independently demonstrate near-identical behavior beyond ordinary agreement among accurate classifiers. Error-set IoU omits which incorrect labels are predicted, and PCA decision slices cover only a restricted input subspace. These limitations warrant more qualified behavioral claims.

The causal explanations remain suggestive. Memorizing random weights establishes capacity to memorize, but does not prove that trained-weight generation learns no meaningful structure. Likewise, failed permutation augmentation does not isolate inadequate structural priors from optimization difficulty. The unsuccessful capacity-reduction experiments in Table 9 further limit attribution to overparameterization.

The scope of several conclusions exceeds the evaluated configurations. G.pt is tested primarily on MNIST under one-step zero-loss conditioning, HyperDiffusion on airplanes, and the main p-diff experiment generates only the last two batch-normalization layers. Comparisons against independently trained full networks partly reflect this restricted p-diff setup. The evidence supports an audit of these configurations more strongly than a general verdict on current weight generation.

Some evaluation details limit reproducibility and precision. Appendix B does not clearly document the construction and sizes of all holdout sets, and its explanation of the saturated HyperDiffusion statistic refers to training-to-training distances despite defining a holdout-based test. Baseline comparisons rely mainly on scatterplots of 100 samples without uncertainty estimates or quantified matched-novelty differences. These are meaningful limitations for close comparisons, although they do not negate the large near-copying effects.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution: downstream accuracy or reconstruction quality alone can conceal copying in weight generators. Studying four established methods across classification and neural fields makes this relevant to both computer vision and evaluation of generative models.

The strongest copying evidence is convincing and supported by complementary measurements. For HyperDiffusion, 94.4% of generated checkpoints lie within L2 distance 10 of a training checkpoint, while all training pairs are separated by more than 50. Corresponding reconstructed shapes closely match, and Appendix B reports a strongly negative data-copying statistic. Appendix C includes examples across distance percentiles, strengthening the evidence beyond selected visualizations.

The simple baselines provide actionable findings. Noise addition achieves competitive accuracy–novelty trade-offs for three methods, while checkpoint averaging competes with p-diff. The analysis acknowledges that p-diff outperforms noise addition before investigating a more appropriate baseline. These findings have value without introducing a new architecture or improving benchmark accuracy.

The investigation goes substantially beyond the initial observation, including data scaling, random-weight training, model-size and regularization changes, symmetry transformations, and an ImageNet extension. Increasing G.pt's training data preserves approximately 94% accuracy while substantially reducing the nearest-neighbor distance gap, providing a constructive result. Overall, the supported empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the interpretive reservations below.
weaknesses: The claim that p-diff generates by 'interpolation, not generalization' is stronger than the evidence. Concentrated parameter marginals, t-SNE overlap, and comparable baseline performance do not establish that generated checkpoints are interpolations of training checkpoints. Independent per-parameter Gaussian sampling is not generally a convex interpolation either. Moreover, interpolation can produce novel, useful functions. The experiments support limited added value over inexpensive baselines more clearly than they establish memorization or its mechanism.

Behavioral similarity does not uniformly provide strong evidence of copying. In Table 4, G.pt's generated-to-training prediction overlap is 98.2%, versus 97.9% between independently trained models. Thus, its behavioral evidence is much weaker than Hyper-Representations' 98.5% versus 75.6%. Error-set IoU also ignores which incorrect labels are predicted, and two-dimensional PCA decision plots provide only a restricted view of model behavior. Conclusions should distinguish the strength of evidence across methods.

Some comparisons change the object being evaluated. Hyper-Representations is compared against autoencoder reconstructions rather than original training checkpoints, despite substantial reconstruction-induced accuracy degradation. This supports copying of reconstructed prototypes but does not directly establish equivalent similarity to the original trained functions. For p-diff, only the last two batch-normalization layers are generated; comparing their diversity with independently trained networks is not a like-for-like expectation of attainable diversity.

The proposed causes remain hypotheses rather than established explanations. Memorizing random weights demonstrates capacity but does not prove that the model learns no meaningful structure from trained weights. Failed permutation augmentation shows a limitation of that training setup, without establishing that symmetry-aware architectures would resolve it. The manuscript sometimes uses categorical language despite these qualifications and despite its own successful G.pt scaling result.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are incomplete for several central experiments. The construction and training budget of the expanded G.pt dataset, the implementation of exhaustive permutation matching, and the holdout construction for Appendix B need more detail. Figures 6 and 8 primarily show sample clouds without uncertainty across independent generator training runs, limiting conclusions about small trade-off differences. The abstract's project/code availability statement also contains no usable link in the supplied manuscript.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution by showing why downstream accuracy alone is insufficient to evaluate weight generators. Its analysis is relevant to both image classifiers and generative neural fields, and the proposed comparisons could improve evaluation practice.

The evidence for near-copying is compelling in several settings. For HyperDiffusion, 94.4% of generated checkpoints lie within L2 distance 10 of training checkpoints, whereas all training pairs are separated by more than 50. Similar reconstructed shapes, behavioral comparisons, and the supplementary data-copying tests reinforce the weight-space evidence.

The simple baselines are a particular strength. Gaussian perturbations expose limited advantages for three methods, while checkpoint averaging and fitted Gaussian sampling provide competitive alternatives to p-diff. Appendix I extends the latter comparison to ImageNet.

The investigation goes beyond documenting failures: data scaling, random-weight experiments, architecture and regularization variations, and symmetry tests probe possible explanations. Reporting that larger datasets alleviate memorization for G.pt but not Hyper-Representations provides useful nuance.

Overall, the supported diagnostic contribution favors acceptance. The paper is clearly organized and offers substantial supplementary evidence; its value does not depend on introducing a new architecture or improving benchmark accuracy.
weaknesses: The p-diff mechanism claim exceeds the evidence. Similar parameter marginals, t-SNE proximity, and comparable accuracy–novelty trade-offs do not establish that generated checkpoints are interpolations of training checkpoints. Independently sampling parameter-wise Gaussians is also not necessarily interpolation. The evidence supports competitiveness of simple baselines more strongly than the categorical claim of 'interpolation, not generalization.'

Behavioral evidence is uneven across methods. In Table 4, G.pt's prediction overlap with its nearest training model is 98.2%, versus 97.9% between training models, providing little separation on this metric. Error IoU also depends on accuracy, and two-dimensional PCA decision regions are limited probes of behavior on realistic inputs. These qualifications matter when extending strong weight-space findings to claims of functional replication.

The scope is narrower than some conclusions suggest. Most methods are evaluated in one primary configuration; p-diff's CIFAR-100 experiment generates only the last two batch-normalization layers. Hyper-Representations is compared primarily against autoencoder-reconstructed checkpoints, so its findings describe replication within a lossy reconstruction space. These are reasonable experimental choices but limit claims about weight generation generally.

The causal explanations remain provisional. Memorizing randomized checkpoints establishes capacity to memorize, not absence of learned structure on real checkpoints. Likewise, failed permutation augmentation does not establish that symmetry-aware architectures would resolve memorization. The successful G.pt scaling experiment offers stronger intervention evidence than these broader mechanistic interpretations.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Appendix B introduces a holdout-based test without clearly documenting holdout construction for every setting, and the new scaling experiments lack sufficient dataset-generation detail. Baseline comparisons rely mainly on scatterplots without uncertainty across independent generator-training runs. These limitations weaken precise equivalence and causal claims, although they do not erase the large observed near-copying effects.
